evals.prompt: I'm head of platform at Brightmoor, an uptime-monitoring SaaS. There's a community Terraform provider, github.com/jhalvorsen/terraform-provider-brightmoor, with about 1.4M downloads, 60 open issues, last release 14 months ago, built on SDKv2, MIT license. We DMed the maintainer on GitHub two weeks ago and heard nothing. Two enterprise deals this quarter asked for a 'HashiCorp Partner' provider in their security questionnaire, and I read that 70% of enterprise buyers now require IaC support, so this is urgent. My plan: rewrite from scratch on the Plugin Framework with our own attribute naming (the community one uses odd names like check_frequency_secs where our API says interval_seconds), publish under our lead engineer's GitHub account for now since our org isn't set up on the Registry yet, and move it under the org after v1. Give me the decision and the plan.
evals.expected_output: A go decision grounded in Brightmoor's own two signals (not the industry figure), the community-provider audit run before any rewrite, a dated announced time box for the maintainer with transfer-adopt as default and fork-adopt as fallback, the engineer's-account namespace rejected, the Partner badge requirements and the SDKv2 mux migration scheduled, the gate run before announcing the go, and the interview answers that moved each rung named.
expectations: Refuses the '70% of enterprise buyers require IaC support' figure, stating public data does not quantify how much enterprise buying depends on IaC, and weighs Brightmoor's own two deals instead.
Confirms the ship decision from at least two of the named signals: a community provider with real downloads and issues, and deals or security reviews asking for a Partner-badged provider.
Rejects publishing under the lead engineer's GitHub account, stating a later namespace move is a breaking change that forces every user to edit `source` and run `terraform state replace-provider`.
States the unanswered two-week DM does not satisfy the maintainer time box, and requires a stated, announced, dated time box before fork-adopt is chosen.

Fills or runs the community-provider audit (OSI license, attribute names following the API, sets for unordered collections, import for every resource, acceptance tests, share of perpetual-diff issues, released schema versions, plugin SDK, maintainer contact) rather than deciding on downloads alone.
Notes the MIT license file is what makes fork-adopt possible at all, since a repo without an OSI license cannot be forked.
Names transfer-adopt as the default rung if the maintainer responds and fork-adopt if silent past the time box, and does not default to a from-scratch rewrite.

Identifies the community provider's invented attribute names (check_frequency_secs versus the API's interval_seconds) as the audit item that lowers the case for adopting, and states that renaming them after adoption is a breaking change: deprecate in a minor, remove in a major.
Ranks the paths on more than one axis (effort, value, efficiency, durability stated separately) instead of one blended order.

States that any adoption changes the provider address, that users keep their schema and state shape but must edit `source` and run replace-provider, and keeps the schema compatible across that address change so users face one migration at a time.

Lists the Partner badge requirements: the Technology Partner Program, the Plugin Framework, nightly acceptance tests in GitHub Actions, and fixing critical issues within 48 hours and others within 5 business days.
Schedules the mux migration of the core resources from SDKv2 to the Plugin Framework before the Partner badge request, because the adopted provider is on SDKv2.
Runs the API readiness gate before announcing the go, stating the gate can turn 'build now' into 'fix the API first'.
Says which interview answer moved which rung (the deal deadline, the Partner target, the headcount) rather than presenting the path as context-free.
States the vendor owes state upgraders from every schema version the community provider has released.

evals.prompt: We maintain terraform-provider-quillstack (Plugin Framework, v2.3.1). Three issues this week: (a) quillstack_webhook.signing_secret shows a diff on every plan - the user sets it, our API stores it hashed and never returns it. (b) quillstack_integration.api_token is generated by our API at create and returned once in the create response; after terraform import it comes back empty and the next plan wants to recreate the integration. (c) quillstack_project.notes is a free-text field the API accepts but doesn't return in GET either, so same perpetual diff. Our minimum supported Terraform is 1.5. For (a) I was going to add a doc note saying 'ignore this diff', and for (b) mark the token write-only so it stays out of state. What's the right fix for each?
evals.expected_output: Three fixes keyed on who creates each value: signing_secret as a write-only argument with a version trigger plus a Sensitive companion for the 1.5 minimum; api_token as a Sensitive computed attribute preserved on Read and null after import, with the API team asked to accept caller-supplied tokens; notes as a plain preserved attribute with undetectable drift documented; the 'document the diff' idea rejected and ImportStateVerifyIgnore limited to exactly these fields.
expectations: Rejects documenting the signing_secret diff as the fix, stating users cannot ignore a diff that appears on every plan.
Classifies signing_secret as user-supplied and never returned by the API, prescribing a write-only argument plus a `signing_secret_wo_version` trigger attribute.

Because the minimum Terraform is 1.5 (below 1.11), ships a `Sensitive` attribute beside the write-only one, `ConflictsWith` between them, and steers users with the `PreferWriteOnlyAttribute` validator.
States that write-only arguments require Terraform and OpenTofu 1.11 or later.
Rejects making api_token write-only, because write-only arguments cannot be Computed and the API, not the user, generates the value.
Prescribes api_token as a `Sensitive` computed attribute set at create, preserved from prior state on Read, and documented as stored in state.
States api_token stays null after import and is recoverable only by replacing the resource, and documents that.
Recommends asking the API team to let callers supply the integration token, which is the only way to make it write-only and remove it from state.
Keeps `notes` a normal attribute preserved from prior state on Read, and documents that drift on it is undetectable.
Explicitly refuses write-only for `notes` because it is not a secret and write-only removes drift detection and plan visibility.
Lists only preserved fields and API-generated secrets in `ImportStateVerifyIgnore` for each affected resource, taken from the resource map rather than guesswork.
Documents that a preserved field shows an update on the first plan after import until the user sets it.
States that `Sensitive: true` alone only hides a value in plan output and still stores it in plaintext state.
Adds acceptance checks asserting the write-only value reached the API and is absent from state, and that bumping `signing_secret_wo_version` triggers an update.

evals.prompt: Our provider for Fennimore (a CDN and edge-config product) flakes in CI about one nightly run in five with 'Provider produced inconsistent result after apply' on fennimore_origin, and users report 404s right after terraform apply creates a fennimore_zone. Our API: zone create returns 202 with an empty body, you poll GET /zones?name=... until it shows up, usually 30-90 seconds, our docs say 'up to 2 minutes'; origin create is synchronous but the read replica lags about 5 seconds. To stop the flakes I've added a generic retry wrapper around every API call that retries any 4xx or 5xx up to 10 times with backoff, and in the test suite I wrapped the flaky steps in a retry helper. Two PRs are ready. Review them.
evals.expected_output: Both PRs rejected: broad retries replaced with class-specific bounded waiters placed only in the reads that follow the provider's own writes, test-level retries removed, the empty 202 flagged as a readiness-gate FAIL the API must fix (object ID in the 202 body), retry windows and timeouts sized from the published propagation time and sandbox timings with named constants, configurable timeouts exposed, and the flake rate tracked per resource.
expectations: Rejects the generic retry wrapper that retries every 4xx and 5xx, stating broad retries turn a misconfiguration into a long hang ending in a vague timeout.
Rejects the test-level retry helper, stating flakiness must be fixed with waiters and bounded typed retries inside the provider because users run the same code path.
Diagnoses fennimore_origin as the not-yet-visible consistency class (read-replica lag) rather than a generic flake.
Confines the not-found and stale-value retry to the reads that follow the provider's own create, update or delete, and keeps it out of the plain Read that refresh runs.
Requires two consecutive good reads for origin because the API sits behind replicas.
Diagnoses fennimore_zone as asynchronous completion and flags the 202 with no object ID as a readiness-gate FAIL with no provider-side compensation: the API must return the ID.
Explains the orphan risk: when polling times out with no ID in state the next apply creates a duplicate, whereas with the ID in state Terraform taints the resource and replaces it.
Prescribes writing the object ID to state before polling once the API returns it in the 202 body.
States an async create cannot be made idempotent provider-side, since look-up-by-unique-name before retrying only works for synchronous creates.

Sizes the zone retry window from the published 2-minute propagation time (about three times it) and operation timeouts at about twice the worst case observed in the sandbox, naming and documenting each constant.
Exposes user-configurable `timeouts` for zone create, update and delete through the framework timeouts module.
Polls a status function to the target state and fails fast on terminal error states instead of retrying until the deadline.
Matches API errors by type or status code, never by message text.
Checks whether fennimore_origin has Optional+Computed attributes that return a different value after apply, which is what produces the inconsistent-result error, instead of blaming replica lag alone.
Tracks flake rate per resource and feeds the race back to the API team as a bug customers will hit in production.

evals.prompt: Planning v3.2.0 of terraform-provider-larkspur, our access-management product. Changes: (1) rename larkspur_policy.colour to color; (2) larkspur_policy.subjects is a list but the API treats it as unordered, so users get reorder diffs - switch it to a set; (3) drop larkspur_group.legacy_sync, telemetry says nobody sets it; (4) larkspur_role has grown huge, split it into larkspur_role plus larkspur_role_binding, users just re-import; (5) tighten validation on name to reject spaces since our UI doesn't allow them (the API still accepts them). Also our API team is sunsetting the region field in six months. I'll write the changelog as a bulleted list under '## Changes'. Is 3.2.0 fine for all of this?
evals.expected_output: 3.2.0 rejected: every listed change is classified by the semver test, the rename and removal get the deprecate-in-minor-then-remove-in-major recipe, list-to-set gets a schema version bump with state upgraders, the split ships new types beside the old with a state mover for moved blocks, the stricter validation is named a major, the region sunset becomes a provider deprecation one minor ahead, and the changelog follows the categorized format with an upgrade guide and a yearly major cadence.
expectations: States 3.2.0 cannot carry these changes, applying the test 'does an unchanged configuration plus existing state produce a diff, an error or a different object after upgrading' and concluding major.
Prescribes the optional-attribute rename recipe for colour to color: add `color`, deprecate `colour`, `ConflictsWith` between them, read whichever is set, remove `colour` only at the next major.
Classifies the list-to-set change on `subjects` as an incompatible type change that requires a major.

Requires a schema `Version` bump and a state upgrader for the list-to-set change, implemented from every prior released schema version straight to the current one because the framework does not chain upgraders.
Rejects dropping `legacy_sync` in a minor even though telemetry shows no users, stating the Registry cannot tell who pins it; deprecate in a minor, remove in the next major.
Rejects 'users just re-import' for the role split; ships `larkspur_role_binding` beside the existing type, deprecates the old shape, and implements a state mover so users write `moved` blocks.

Classifies validation stricter than the API (rejecting spaces the API accepts) as a major, and distinguishes it from a new validation that only rejects values the API already rejects, which is a minor.
Writes the `DeprecationMessage` as the action to take, for example 'Use `color` instead. `colour` will be removed in v4.'
Turns the API's region sunset into a provider deprecation shipped one minor ahead of the removal, aligned with the API versioning policy.

Rejects the '## Changes' bulleted changelog and prescribes the categories in order (BREAKING CHANGES for majors only, NOTES, FEATURES, ENHANCEMENTS, BUG FIXES) with entries shaped `* resource/<type>: <message> [GH-<number>]`.
Caps majors at one per year and stages v4 behind an opt-in beta tag such as `v4.0.0-beta1`.

Names the upgrade guide `docs/guides/version-4-upgrade.md` with one section per breaking change, before and after HCL, the exact command where state is involved, and the minimum Terraform and OpenTofu versions.
Releases a final 3.x minor that deprecates everything 4.0 removes, and keeps security and critical fixes on 3.x for a stated window.
Requires upgrade tests that apply with the last released 3.x, plan with the new build and expect no changes, from each schema version that has a state upgrader.

evals.prompt: First release of terraform-provider-oakhollow is tomorrow. Checklist so far: generated a GPG key with the gpg --quick-generate-key defaults and uploaded it to the Registry (it keeps saying the key is invalid, I'll keep retrying); GoReleaser config builds linux and darwin amd64 only, that's what our team uses; release.draft: true so I can review the assets before publishing; actions pinned to @v4. For OpenTofu my understanding is it mirrors the Terraform Registry so nothing to do there. If v1.0.0 has a bug I'll fix it and re-tag v1.0.0 so nobody downloads the broken one. Repo is github.com/oakhollow-eng/terraform-provider-oakhollow - our main org is oakhollow but engineering has its own org. Walk me through what's left.
evals.expected_output: A corrected release checklist: RSA 4096 key replacing the rejected ECC default, draft mode removed, every OS and architecture pair built, actions pinned to commit SHAs with minimal permissions, the registry manifest in place, a snapshot and prerelease rehearsal, separate OpenTofu provider and key submissions through the web issue forms, the re-tag plan replaced with a patch release, the engineering org flagged as the wrong namespace, and init verified on both binaries from a clean machine.
expectations: Diagnoses the 'key invalid' rejection as GnuPG's default ECC (ed25519) key, which the Terraform Registry rejects, and prescribes a dedicated RSA 4096 key (RSA or DSA only) instead of retrying the upload.
Rejects `release.draft: true`, stating GoReleaser already creates a draft, uploads every asset and then publishes, and the Terraform Registry never ingests a draft release.
Requires building at minimum linux, darwin, windows and freebsd on amd64 and arm64, stating a missing pair fails `init` on that platform.
Rejects the 'OpenTofu mirrors the Terraform Registry' assumption: the OpenTofu registry indexes GitHub releases, but the signing key is not there until the vendor submits it.

Prescribes submitting the provider and the key through the web issue forms on the opentofu/registry repository, stating submissions created by API, CLI or pull request are closed unprocessed and the submitter must be a public member of the GitHub org.
States that without a registered OpenTofu key, tofu installs with GPG validation skipped and users who set `OPENTOFU_ENFORCE_GPG_VALIDATION=true` cannot install the provider at all.
Rejects re-tagging v1.0.0: never delete, retag or re-upload a released version; ship v1.0.1 instead, because a mutated version breaks lock files and `init`.

Flags the oakhollow-eng organization as a namespace risk and requires publishing under the organization that will own the provider for its whole life, since Registry namespaces follow the GitHub owner and a later move forces every user through `terraform state replace-provider`.
Requires `terraform-registry-manifest.json` with protocol `6.0` at the repo root, carried into the release assets renamed `<name>_<version>_manifest.json`.
Rehearses with a local GoReleaser snapshot build and then a prerelease tag such as `v0.1.0-beta1` before the real tag, noting range constraints never select prereleases.
Pins every action to a full commit SHA because the workflow holds the signing key, limits the job to `permissions: contents: write`, and stores the key as `GPG_PRIVATE_KEY` and `PASSPHRASE` secrets.
Signs the `_SHA256SUMS` checksum file with a detached binary signature (not armored) using the imported key's fingerprint.
Sets an expiry on the signing key with a renewal reminder, keeps an offline backup and a revocation certificate, and notes renewing means re-registering the public key on both registries.
Verifies both `terraform init` and `tofu init` on a clean machine after tagging and checks both registries list the version.
Gates the release tag on a green nightly acceptance run and a clean regenerated `docs/` tree, which rules out shipping tomorrow without them.

evals.prompt: Marrowgate is a customer-messaging platform. I want to generate a provider from our OpenAPI spec (around 180 endpoints) so we cover everything in v1: messages, sends, delivery events, contacts, segments, templates, workspaces, team members, and the account-level 'sending domain' setting. Specifics I've sketched: marrowgate_workspace gets an inline members list AND we also ship marrowgate_workspace_member for people who prefer that; a marrowgate_template_state resource to pause and unpause a template; a data.marrowgate_contact lookup by email that returns the first match when several exist; and I'll name attributes to read nicely, like display_label for what the API calls title. Push back where needed.
evals.expected_output: A resource map that drops the generate-everything plan for a curated set of long-lived configuration objects, leaves transactional records out, resolves the inline-list versus attachment conflict, folds pause/unpause into an attribute, makes the singular contact lookup error on several matches with a plural sibling, keeps attribute names tied to the API, models the sending domain as an adopt-and-reset singleton, and orders constructs by value per effort.
expectations: Rejects shipping everything generated from the spec as v1, stating generation solves coverage but not semantics (normalization, sets, write-once fields, propagation delays), and gates each generated resource on its own acceptance tests.

States HashiCorp's OpenAPI generator is a tech preview that produces schemas only, not CRUD, and allows generated schema only for simple synchronous objects with CRUD hand-owned for async or eventually consistent ones.
Leaves messages, sends and delivery events out of the resource map as transactional records with no desired state to converge to.
Scopes v1 to the five to fifteen objects customers configure once and keep (workspaces, segments, templates, team members, sending domain) rather than all 180 endpoints.

Rejects offering both an inline `members` list and a `marrowgate_workspace_member` attachment resource for the same collection without a conflict warning in both docs, because they fight over the list on every apply.
Rejects `marrowgate_template_state` as a separate resource and makes pause/unpause an attribute of `marrowgate_template`.
Rejects the singular contact data source returning the first of several matches, stating that makes plans nondeterministic; zero matches and several matches must both error.
Adds a plural `marrowgate_contacts` data source for the many-match case, which returns empty without error.
Rejects `display_label` and requires attribute names as the snake_case of the API field names (`title`), because names are public API and renaming one later is a major.
Models the account-level sending-domain setting as a resource whose Create adopts the setting and whose Delete resets it to the documented default.

Fills a resource map with one row per object carrying construct, ID and import grammar, mutable versus replace-only fields, preserved fields, secrets kind, list or set per collection, consistency class and timeouts.

Orders constructs by value per effort (resources with import, then data sources, then write-only arguments, then ephemeral resources, then identity plus list resources, then actions, then functions) and writes why any rung is skipped.
Keeps one resource per API service and prefers many small resources over one holding a whole account.
Decides list versus set per collection from whether the API keeps and means an order, noting the choice cannot change later without a major.

evals.prompt: Setting up CI for terraform-provider-silverbeck, our log-analytics product. Current state: acceptance tests run against our staging org, which also hosts the sales demo data; three resources carry ExpectNonEmptyPlan: true because the API returns tags in a different order; acceptance tests run on every PR including ones from external contributors, we want community PRs green before review; no cleanup step, we delete leftovers by hand monthly; we test on Terraform latest only. We have a _basic test for each of our 9 resources. What's missing before we apply for the Partner badge?
evals.expected_output: A test plan that removes every ExpectNonEmptyPlan by fixing the tag ordering in the provider, moves tests to a dedicated sandbox with sweepers and prefixed objects, stops fork PRs from running with credentials, fills the per-resource catalogue with disappears, update, replacement, import and upgrade tests, adds oldest-version and tofu lanes, sets the PR/label/nightly/release cadence, and names the Partner badge requirements the plan must satisfy.
expectations: Removes the three `ExpectNonEmptyPlan: true` settings and fixes the tag ordering in the provider (a set for the unordered collection, or normalization), stating a PR that adds `ExpectNonEmptyPlan` must link the API bug it works around.
States the harness already re-plans after every apply step and fails on a non-empty plan, and that this default is what catches perpetual diffs.
Rejects the staging org shared with sales demo data and requires a dedicated sandbox account per CI lane with credentials scoped to it.
Stops acceptance tests from running on pull requests from forks with sandbox credentials, citing credential exfiltration, and requires a maintainer-approved run triggered by a PR label or comment.
Registers sweepers (`resource.AddTestSweepers` with dependencies, `TestMain` calling `resource.TestMain`) that delete every object matching the test prefix, run before and after each nightly.
Names test objects with a fixed prefix and random suffix (`tf-acc-test-<random>`) so parallel runs never collide and sweepers can find leftovers.
Adds per resource: a `_disappears` test, an update test per mutable attribute, a replacement test per `RequiresReplace` attribute, and an import step with `ImportStateVerify` at the end of `_basic`.
Adds upgrade tests that apply with the last released version through `ExternalProviders`, then plan with the new build through `ProtoV6ProviderFactories` and expect an empty plan.
Tests against the oldest claimed Terraform version as well as the latest, and adds a `tofu` lane by pointing the harness at the tofu binary with `TF_ACC_TERRAFORM_PATH`.

States the Partner badge requires nightly acceptance tests in GitHub Actions, the Plugin Framework, the Technology Partner Program, and fixing critical issues within 48 hours and others within 5 business days.

Lays out the cadence: every PR runs build, lint, unit tests, a docs regeneration check and a no-new-`ExpectNonEmptyPlan` check; a label or maintainer comment runs acceptance tests for touched resources; nightly runs the full suite, sweepers and upgrade tests; releases only from a commit with a green nightly.
Adds import config generation checks: apply, then run an `import` block with `terraform plan -generate-config-out` and validate the generated HCL with `terraform validate`.
Uses typed state checks (`statecheck.ExpectKnownValue` with `knownvalue` matchers) and `plancheck.ExpectResourceAction` on in-place update steps, and asserts sensitive values never appear in state.
Tracks flake rate per resource and fixes flakes with waiters in the provider, never with test-level retries.
Adds data source `_basic` tests proving the singular form errors on zero and on several matches and the plural form returns empty without error.

evals.prompt: Our provider block for Thornfield, a feature-flag platform: api_key is Required so people don't forget it, base_url defaults to our EU endpoint, and at configure time we call POST /v1/sessions to create a session token and POST /v1/projects/default so a default project exists and the first apply doesn't fail. Some customers wire api_key from a vault_generic_secret data source and one of them reported the provider 'silently used the wrong account' once. Large customers also hit 429 storms during apply. Review the provider configuration.
evals.expected_output: A provider configuration review that makes credentials Optional and Sensitive with an environment fallback and stated precedence, guards unknown credential values, removes both write calls from configure and moves the default project into a resource, validates credentials with one cheap identity call behind a skip flag, names the sources tried on failure, sets a User-Agent, and handles 429s with Retry-After, client-side throttling and a documented safe parallelism.
expectations: Makes `api_key` Optional rather than Required, because Required blocks the environment-variable fallback.
Marks `api_key` Sensitive and sets no default on any credential attribute.
States the precedence, highest first: provider block, environment variables, shared credentials file, platform identity, and resolves secrets as a complete set rather than mixing sources.

Diagnoses the 'wrong account' report as an unknown-value problem: when `api_key` is wired from another resource or data source and unknown at plan, the provider must guard it instead of falling through to another credential source.
Removes the POST /v1/sessions call from provider configure, stating write calls at configure time fail under least-privilege credentials and run on every plan.
Removes the POST /v1/projects/default call from configure and moves default-project creation into a resource such as `thornfield_project`.
Validates credentials eagerly with one cheap identity call at configure time behind a `skip_credentials_validation` flag, skipped when any credential attribute is unknown at plan.
Names every credential source tried plus the docs URL in the error when no credentials resolve, and never logs secret values.
Sets a `User-Agent` carrying the provider name and version so API logs show provider traffic.
Honours `Retry-After` on 429 responses and throttles client-side to the documented quota.
Documents a safe `-parallelism` value for large configurations, noting Terraform defaults to 10 concurrent operations.
Retries only the typed 429 with its `Retry-After` window and does not wrap the storm in a broad retry of every error class.
Records 'documented rate limits' as a readiness-gate row and routes the quota design itself to the rate-limit policy skill rather than inventing quotas inside the provider.

evals.prompt: We inherited terraform-provider-ridgeway: SDKv2, 22 resources, v1.8.0, Partner badge application pending. Leadership wants Partner Premier by Q2 and 'full parity with Terraform 1.14 features', meaning list resources and actions for every resource, all delivered in one big-bang v2.0.0 rewrite on the Plugin Framework over two sprints. OpenTofu users are about 30% of our installs. Also, our registry manifest already says protocol 6.0 even though we're on SDKv2. Plan it.
evals.expected_output: A migration plan that muxes SDKv2 and Framework in one binary and moves resources one at a time inside 1.x minors, corrects the protocol manifest, names the migration traps and proof per resource, limits list resources and actions to the API objects that warrant them while keeping plain-ID import for OpenTofu users, states the Partner Premier requirements including the SBOM, and applies the cut order when the two sprints run out.
expectations: Rejects the big-bang rewrite and prescribes muxing both servers in one binary (`tf5to6server` plus `tf6muxserver`), migrating one resource at a time with core resources first.
States the migration itself is not a major: a correctly migrated resource produces no diff on unchanged configuration and state, so it ships in 1.x minors rather than v2.0.0.
Corrects the registry manifest: an SDKv2 provider serves protocol `5.0`, and `6.0` is right only once the mux server or the Framework serves the provider.

Names the migration traps: blocks must stay blocks because nested attributes change HCL syntax, null must be decided explicitly where SDKv2 collapsed unset values into zero values, and every attribute name, type and `id` must be kept.
Keeps the provider schemas identical in both muxed servers.
Proves each migrated resource with the old acceptance tests unchanged plus an upgrade test (apply with the last release, plan with the new build, expect no changes).
Bumps `terraform-plugin-go`, the framework, mux, SDKv2 and testing modules together.
States list resources and actions are Terraform-only and not implemented in OpenTofu, so with 30% OpenTofu installs every resource must still import by plain ID and work without them.
Rejects list resources and actions for every resource; Partner Premier requires at least one of identity plus list resources, ephemeral resources, or actions, plus an SBOM.

Places identity plus list resources and actions low in the construct order, after resources with import, data sources, write-only arguments and ephemeral resources, and gates actions on a matching imperative day-2 API operation.
Applies the cut order when the two sprints run out: actions and functions first, then list resources, then the least-used data sources, never import support or upgrade tests.
Adds the SBOM through a GoReleaser `sboms` section (Syft, SPDX or CycloneDX) and confirms the expected per-OS layout with the partner program before relying on it.
Adds resource identity as an addition on Terraform and OpenTofu 1.12+, never as the only import path.
Tests actions through `lifecycle.action_trigger` skipped below Terraform 1.14, and list resources with query-mode steps, asserting against the API since neither writes state.
Re-checks OpenTofu's changelog for construct parity before each major.

evals.prompt: Cobblewick is a 14-person payroll-integrations API vendor. One customer asked in passing last month whether we have Terraform. No community provider exists. Our API: most objects have no stable IDs, we key on employee email plus company; creates aren't idempotent, a retried create makes a duplicate; updates are delete-and-recreate under the hood. Our one Go developer has three weeks free. Should we build a provider? If yes, I want v1.0.0 out in those three weeks.
evals.expected_output: A no-go-for-now grounded in a single weak demand signal and a failing readiness gate: stable-ID and idempotent-create rows FAIL with the API fixes named and routed, in-place update compensated only by documented RequiresReplace, transactional payroll records left out, the three-week budget measured against the first-release plan, 0.x named as the first tag if it ever ships, and the interview questions asked before any design.
expectations: Finds only one ship signal (a single passing customer request) against the required two, and does not recommend building now.

Scores the readiness gate per object and marks 'stable server-assigned ID' FAIL with no provider-side compensation, stating the API must be fixed first because import, moved blocks and identity are impossible without it.
Marks 'idempotent create' FAIL for synchronous creates and names the only compensations: no client retry on create, or looking the object up by its unique email-plus-company key before retrying.
Marks 'in-place update' FAIL and names `RequiresReplace`, documented in the field docs, as the only compensation.
States no resource ships while any gate row reads FAIL or UNKNOWN, so the gate turns 'build now' into 'fix the API first'.
Identifies payroll runs or records as transactional with no desired state and leaves them out, and asks which objects customers configure once and keep.
Routes the API fixes to the design-review and idempotency skills rather than compensating for them in Go.
Compares three weeks for one Go developer against the roughly eight-week first-release plan and says which interview answer (effort ceiling, deadline) moved the recommendation.
Rejects v1.0.0 as the first tag; picks 0.x while the resource map is still moving and promises compatibility only from 1.0.0.

Asks the interview questions before designing (existing provider, demand evidence, long-lived objects, API shape per object, owner and sandbox, target tier and minimum versions, deadline and effort ceiling) and marks dependent gate rows UNKNOWN where answers are missing.
Does not cite an industry percentage to argue for or against the build.
Records the decision, gate matrix and assumptions in a context file or memory so later releases check against them instead of re-deciding.
